prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the lumbar puncture before imaging has excluded a mass lesion with midline shift, and involve neurosurgery first for the communicating hydrocephalus — the puncture is required, but its timing and the ICP plan are not optional
Do NOT proceed to lumbar puncture: imaging shows mass effect / significant hydrocephalus and LP risks cerebral herniation until ICP is managed and neurosurgery has cleared the procedure.
Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do NOT perform lumbar puncture before CT head when any imaging-first criterion (altered mental status, focal deficit, papilledema, seizure, immunocompromise, age >60) is present.

Do NOT discontinue dexamethasone solely because the Gram stain is negative — completion of the 4-day course is appropriate in suspected pneumococcal meningitis until alternative organism is identified.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
Do NOT use steroids without simultaneously starting anti-tuberculous therapy.
Do NOT rely on a negative AFB smear to exclude TBM; sensitivity is low and MTB PCR / culture are required.
required_recommendations: Initiate empiric four-drug anti-tuberculous therapy (RIPE: rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) within hours of clinical suspicion.
Administer adjunctive dexamethasone 0.4 mg/kg/day IV with taper over 6-8 weeks (or per latest guideline) for TBM with neurologic deficits.
Send CSF AFB stain, MTB PCR (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra), mycobacterial culture, and ADA before steroid initiation alters cellularity.
Consult neurosurgery early for hydrocephalus management (CSF diversion may be required).
Initiate HIV testing and screen for systemic TB foci (chest imaging, sputum).
Report case to public health and trace close contacts.

avoided_actions.rationale: No evidence of endocarditis as a primary source in this case; echocardiography is not part of routine meningitis workup.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to meningitis diagnosis or treatment.
PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

differential.key_features: Would expect higher PMN predominance (>80%) and more acute course; this case shows lymphocyte-predominant CSF over 2-week onset with basilar enhancement
Lymphocytic CSF with low glucose can mimic TBM; India ink and cryptococcal antigen testing are required to exclude
Basilar leptomeningeal enhancement and lymphocytic CSF overlap with TBM; ACE level and systemic features needed
Typically normal CSF glucose and self-limited course; the markedly low CSF glucose and elevated protein argue against viral etiology
Diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement can mimic TBM; CSF cytology and the lack of known malignancy reduce likelihood

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus without a mass lesion or midline shift is not a contraindication to lumbar puncture; a space-occupying lesion with shift is. Reading 'raised intracranial pressure' as a prohibition removes the test that makes the diagnosis and, in cryptococcal disease, the treatment that lowers the pressure.
Subacute lymphocyte-predominant CSF with very low glucose and high protein in a patient from a high-prevalence area should prompt TBM workup, not pyogenic meningitis treatment alone.
Basal cistern and tentorial enhancement plus ring-enhancing basal-ganglia lesions (tuberculomas) is a near-pathognomonic imaging pattern for TBM.
MTB PCR (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra) has higher sensitivity than AFB smear; ADA elevation supports TBM in the right clinical context.
Adjunctive corticosteroids reduce mortality in TBM and must be initiated together with anti-tuberculous therapy.
Hydrocephalus is common in TBM and warrants neurosurgical involvement.
WHO 2025: obtain cultures promptly, but neither LP nor cranial imaging may delay empirical antimicrobials when the pathway requires treatment first.

clinical_pearls: CSF glucose:serum ratio <0.3 with lymphocytic predominance is highly suggestive of TB meningitis
GeneXpert TB PCR on CSF has ~60-80% sensitivity and >95% specificity — a positive result is diagnostic
Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TB meningitis (Thwaites et al., NEJM 2004)
Choroidal tubercles on fundoscopy are pathognomonic for disseminated TB
TB meningitis without active pulmonary TB is well-recognized — hematogenous reactivation from latent foci
metadata.diagnostic_challenge: Subacute meningitis initially treated as bacterial but cultures negative. Lymphocytic CSF with very low glucose and basilar enhancement on MRI point to TB meningitis in a patient with epidemiologic risk factors. Low procalcitonin, BCG history, and absence of pulmonary symptoms may mislead.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Priya Sharma is a 42-year-old right-handed Indian-born woman (US resident for 15 years) who presents to the emergency department with a 2-week history of progressively worsening headache, low-grade fevers, malaise, and increasing confusion. She returned from a 3-week visit to her family in rural Maharashtra, India approximately 6 weeks prior to presentation. The headache began insidiously as a dull, generalized ache that she initially attributed to jet lag and stress from returning to work. Over the first week, the headache intensified and she developed low-grade fevers with a maximum temperature of 38.3°C, night sweats, and decreased appetite with unintentional weight loss of approximately 4 kg. She was seen at an urgent care center 5 days ago, where she was diagnosed with sinusitis and prescribed amoxicillin 875 mg twice daily. Her symptoms continued to worsen despite the antibiotic. Three days ago, her husband noted she was increasingly confused, forgetting conversations and asking the same questions repeatedly. Two days ago, she developed new-onset diplopia (seeing double when looking to either side) and worsening photophobia. Yesterday, her husband noticed asymmetry in her face with drooping on the left side. He brought her to the emergency department this morning when she could not recall the current date or her children's school names. She denies cough, hemoptysis, or pulmonary symptoms. She denies rash, joint pains, or visual loss. She has no history of HIV testing but denies risk factors. She had BCG vaccination in childhood in India. Her paternal uncle died of tuberculosis in India 10 years ago, but she reports no known direct exposure to active TB cases.
